title: How rare are Markovian quantum dynamics?
authors: Charlotte Bäcker, Nick Maryshchak, Walter T. Strunz
abstract: A profound understanding of decoherence and dissipation in quantum dynamics is crucial for the realistic modeling of the evolution of quantum systems. In open quantum dynamics one distinguishes between a memoryless, so-called Markovian evolution and dynamics incorporating memory effects, termed non-Markovian. In this work we study how prevalent memory effects are in the set of all such dynamics. We thus investigate how often a Markovian description is applicable. This question is approached by investigating randomly generated two-step qubit dynamics with respect to different concepts and witnesses of non-Markovianity. We observe that almost all dynamics are non-Markovian, and only a small (yet finite) fraction is Markovian. Furthermore, we study how this proportion changes when considering certain subclasses such as lower rank or mixed-unitary dynamics. Importantly, our results shed light on the relative ratios of -- and interrelations between -- the sets of dynamics that are non-Markovian with respect to different criteria. Finally, we investigate the fraction of dynamics in which the memory effects are necessarily of quantum nature and establish a connection between two recently developed concepts that characterize the quantumness of memory in non-Markovian dynamics.
summary: The paper rigorously investigates the prevalence of non-Markovian dynamics by testing numerous mathematical witnesses across randomly generated two-step quantum processes. It concludes that memory effects are the generic feature of open quantum evolution, while also developing tools to distinguish between genuine quantum memory and classical forms of information backflow.
main_problem: The work investigates how frequently quantum dynamics exhibit memory effects (non-Markovianity) compared to simple, history-independent Markovian evolution.
main_result: For randomly generated two-step qubit dynamics, the vast majority of processes are non-Markovian, suggesting that memory effects are the generic case in open quantum systems.
method: The authors analyze the space of two-step quantum maps by testing multiple mathematical criteria (e.g., CP-indivisibility, trace distance increase) to detect deviations from Markovian behavior.
model_or_system: The study focuses on open quantum dynamics for qubits, modeled as a sequence of two time steps ($D=(E_1, E_2)$). The analysis compares these discrete maps against the continuous-time Lindblad/GKSL master equation framework.
key_observables: Non-Markovianity witnesses include CP-indivisibility, violation of Data Processing Inequality (DPI), increase in Bloch volume ($V_{	ext{Bloch}}$), and entanglement measures ($C$).
important_parameters: The maximal Kraus rank ($k_{	ext{max}}$) is a key parameter used to restrict the space of dynamics being analyzed.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on sampling random two-step dynamics or restricting the channels to specific forms, such as mixed-unitary (MU) maps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relationships between various definitions and witnesses for non-Markovianity, and show how the fraction of quantum memory depends on the maximal Kraus rank ($k_{	ext{max}}$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general prevalence of non-Markovianity using random sampling across multiple criteria. It then refines this by examining specific subclasses (like mixed-unitary dynamics) and distinguishing between quantum memory, genuine backflow, and classical memory effects.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous quantitative measure for how often the simple Markov approximation fails in realistic physical scenarios, which is crucial for designing accurate open system models in AMO physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Relations between different definitions and witnesses of quantum non-Markovianity. A solid line from node (A) to (B) means that it is proven that non-Markovianity ac- cording to (A) implies non-Markovianity according to (B). A dashed line means that among our results obtained via random sampling of two-step dynamics any dynamics which turned out to be non-Markovian with respect to (A) was also non-Markovian with respect to (B). Nodes in boldface denote definitions of non-Markovianity while other nodes represent witnesses.

FIG. 2. Physical motivation of the sampling strategy for a dynamics D = (E1, E2) used in this work. A randomly sam- pled first map E1 can be understood as the application of a random global system-environment unitary operation. While in reality, after having implemented E1 the map E2 is realized in terms of a second random unitary operation U12 on system and environment, it suffices to generate a second map E2 inde- pendently. This can be seen by decomposing U12 = U2 ◦U −1 1 , which implies that a randomly generated map corresponding to the consecutive random unitaries U1 and U21 contains the same information as an independently generated map corre- sponding to the unitary U2.
